summary: Yahweh calls Abram away from home with promises of nationhood, land, and blessing extending to all families; Abram travels with Sarai and Lot through Canaan and builds altars. Famine drives them to Egypt, where Abram asks Sarai to say she is his sister, Pharaoh takes her, and plagues lead Pharaoh to confront and expel Abram.
whyItMatters: The promise narrows the story to one family while keeping a worldwide horizon. The Egypt episode immediately tests trust and shows Sarai exposed to danger through Abram’s fear.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: Haran, sites in Canaan including Shechem and Bethel, and Egypt during famine.
context.literaryForm: Call-and-journey narrative with promise and altars followed by a famine-driven deception episode.

before.text: Terah’s family stopped in Haran on a journey toward Canaan, and Sarai was described as childless. Abram’s call begins from that unfinished family situation.

here.text: Keep the promises to Abram in view while following his journey, famine, fear, Sarai’s removal to Pharaoh’s house, and Pharaoh’s protest.

after.text: Abram, Sarai, and Lot return from Egypt, and pressure on shared pasture leads Abram and Lot to separate.

outline.heading: Call and worldwide blessing
outline.note: Yahweh commands departure and promises nation, name, and blessing beyond Abram’s family.

outline.heading: Arrival and worship in Canaan
outline.note: Abram travels with household members and builds altars at promised land sites.

outline.heading: Famine and Abram’s proposed deception
outline.note: Abram goes to Egypt and asks Sarai to identify as his sister for his safety.

outline.heading: Sarai taken and Pharaoh’s house afflicted
outline.note: Officials take Sarai to Pharaoh, Abram gains possessions, and Yahweh strikes the royal house.

outline.heading: Pharaoh confronts and expels Abram
outline.note: Pharaoh identifies Sarai as Abram’s wife, challenges him, and sends the couple away.

keyVerses.text: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who treats you with contempt. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”
keyVerses.why: The blessing is directed through Abram toward all families of the earth.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh appeared to Abram and said, “I will give this land to your offspring.” He built an altar there to Yahweh, who had appeared to him.
keyVerses.why: The land promise appears while Canaanites are already said to live there.

keyVerses.text: The princes of Pharaoh saw her, and praised her to Pharaoh; and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house.
keyVerses.why: Sarai’s removal to Pharaoh’s house is a central cost of Abram’s survival strategy.

questions.question: What is Abram asked to leave?
questions.answer: Yahweh tells him to leave his country, relatives, and father’s house for a land to be shown to him. Abram travels from Haran with Sarai, Lot, possessions, and people acquired there, so departure is a household move rather than a solitary walk.

questions.question: Who is meant to benefit from Abram’s blessing?
questions.answer: The promise says he will become a great nation and that all families of the earth will be blessed through him. It makes this family important within a wider human story rather than naming blessing as theirs alone.

questions.question: Does the land promise say Canaan is empty?
questions.answer: No. The narrative specifically notes Canaanites in the land when Abram arrives and then reports a promise to his offspring. The chapter does not discuss those inhabitants’ consent or resolve later conflicts over the land.

questions.question: What does it mean that Abram lives as a “foreigner” in Egypt?
questions.answer: A severe famine drives him there, and the text describes his residence as temporary and away from his own land. This vulnerable status helps explain his fear, while it does not excuse the danger he creates for Sarai.

questions.question: What happens to Sarai in Pharaoh’s house?
questions.answer: Pharaoh’s officials praise her, and she is taken into his house while Abram receives wealth. The chapter does not record her consent or speech in Egypt, so the episode should not be smoothed into a harmless family strategy.

questions.question: Why does Abram ask Sarai to say she is his sister?
questions.answer: He fears Egyptians will kill him because she is his wife and hopes the sister claim will preserve his life. The passage presents his stated motive but also shows the outcome placing Sarai in Pharaoh’s possession.

questions.question: Why is Pharaoh struck when Abram deceives him?
questions.answer: The narrator says Yahweh afflicts Pharaoh’s house because of Sarai and then records Pharaoh’s complaint that Abram concealed the marriage. It does not explain the fairness of every consequence to Pharaoh or his household.

questions.question: What is an “altar” doing during Abram’s travels?
questions.answer: Abram builds altars at places where Yahweh appears or where he calls on Yahweh’s name. The chapter uses them as worship markers along the journey rather than as proof that he owns the surrounding territory.

glossary.def: A person living temporarily outside their own home region, as Abram does in famine-stricken Egypt.
A constructed place associated here with Abram’s worship of Yahweh along his route.
A severe shortage of food that drives Abram’s household from Canaan into Egypt.
